label: Atlantic
rationale: A live document of what the sources call Mingus's finest working band at its peak: the pianoless quartet of Mingus, Ted Curson, Eric Dolphy and Dannie Richmond, augmented for the night by Booker Ervin and, on one number, Bud Powell — recorded at the Antibes Jazz Festival on 13 July 1960 and issued by Atlantic in 1976 (S1, S2, S3). Reception is unusually unanimous: AllMusic 5 stars, DownBeat 5 stars, Rolling Stone Jazz Record Guide 5 stars, Penguin Guide 4 stars (S1). The lineage case is the record's own: the Atlantic liner notes place its 'freedom-with-order' directly upstream of Anthony Braxton and the Art Ensemble of Chicago, and it was cut three months before the Candid Charles Mingus Presents Charles Mingus with the same core personnel (S1, S3). Session gravity is the point of the album — Dolphy, Ervin and Powell inside one Mingus performance — and it still plays: the band's heat is audible, not archival (S2, S3).

personnel_record.notes: Single live session: 13 July 1960, Antibes Jazz Festival, Juan-les-Pins, France (S1, S2, S3, S4). Album year is the recording year; the Atlantic double LP appeared in 1976 (US 1979 per Wikipedia's narrative; AllMusic dates its entry 1979), after a 1974 Japanese BYG issue as Charles Mingus Live With Eric Dolphy (S1, S2, S3). Producer: Nesuhi Ertegun, credited as executive producer on the Atlantic liner notes (S3) and as executive producer/producer at AllMusic (S2). Engineer is recorded as null: the liner notes name only 'recorded live by Barclay Studios', with no individual engineer; AllMusic's credits tab lists Elliott Federman as engineer, but that credit is attached to the Atlantic reissue package rather than the 1960 concert recording, so it is not asserted here as the session engineer (S2, S3). Track titles follow Wikipedia and the liner notes; AllMusic prints 'Better Get Hit in Yo' Soul' and 'Folk Forms, No. 1' for the same performances. Sides are not given in any source consulted (null); the original issue was a two-record set (S1, S4). Duration 71:44 on CD (S1, S4); AllMusic's 1979 entry totals 1:09:21 for its edition (S2). Mingus takes piano on tracks 1 and 6, and Powell joins on track 4; Ervin sits out track 3 (S1, S3). Liner-note essay is Robert Palmer's (S3).

ballot.case_for: Antibes is a defining live statement of Mingus's freedom-with-order: blues and church-music foundations support collective improvisation without abandoning post-bop structure. The Mingus–Dolphy–Curson–Richmond core, expanded by Booker Ervin and Bud Powell's guest appearance, supplies exceptional session gravity and a distinctive pianoless ensemble sound (S2, S3). AllMusic's direct review and the DownBeat, Rolling Stone, and Penguin ratings compiled in S1 establish broad critical acclaim, while the concert's intensity makes its historical importance immediately audible. Robert Palmer's liner essay connects the band's methods to Braxton and the Art Ensemble of Chicago, supporting a stylistic lineage argument rather than proving this album's direct influence (S3).
ballot.case_against: The recording remained commercially unavailable until the 1970s, so it cannot straightforwardly receive credit for shaping the 1960s dialogue as a released album (S1, S4). Much of its repertoire has competing definitive studio treatments, especially on Blues & Roots, Mingus Ah Um, and Charles Mingus Presents Charles Mingus; its claim must therefore rest on transformative live interplay rather than compositional novelty. Moreover, most of the cross-guide acclaim is supplied through a secondary ratings compilation, not documented canon-list placements, and the specific downstream influence claim rests on one retrospective liner essay.
ballot.disagreement: Neither reference dissents from consensus_core/strong or identifies a genuine scope boundary. Their reservations differ: Reference 1 emphasizes the limits of the consensus and influence evidence, while Reference 2 additionally questions the recording's dynamics and Powell's performance; those latter criticisms are not substantiated by the supplied sources.
ballot.recommendation: The council proposes that John give Antibes strong consideration as a consensus-core live statement, judging its distinctive ensemble achievement rather than treating it as a contemporaneously influential 1960 release.
